{xpost} NASA has reported a localized 'atmosphere' generating over the Ceres lights, how?

If the bright spots are made of ice (the other competing theory I know of is salts), then the ice can sublimate from a solid into a gas creating a localized atmosphere. Ceres is too small to hold onto a global atmosphere, but what they're talking about is basically a crater with ice at the bottom filling that crater up with gas from whatever the ice deposits are. If the atmosphere findings are verified, then they can be fairly certain the bright spots are ices and not salts. I'm not familiar with the instrument package on Dawn, but if they have the right instrumentation, they should be able to determine what type of ice or ices are present.

Also, take a look at the New Horizon mission. They've been making great discoveries already about the ices on Pluto, and as Pluto gets colder and it goes further from the sun, one theory is that the atmosphere would condense back down to ice for the coldest part of the orbit, and then sublimate back into an atmosphere when it gets warmer again. It's too early in their mission to know much for sure yet, but they have measured a lower atmospheric density than they expected (by half), so it's possible that this may be happening right now. New Horizon has raised more questions than answers at this point, but at that distance, it will be something like a year before all the data finishes downloading.

They're currently in the process of studying this, but they believe that the light-coloured spots are ice at the bottom of craters. The ice is subliming into gas, which is held within the rim of the crater like water in a bowl. This creates a highly local "mini-atmosphere", as it were.
